title: NumPy and Vectorized Computation: Arrays, Shapes, and Broadcasting
description: Understand array dimensions and vectorized numerical operations used in data preparation and model inputs.
learningObjectives: Explain NumPy arrays, shape, dimensions, dtype, and axis in concrete examples.
Read vectorized operations and compare them with Python loops.
Predict how broadcasting combines compatible shapes.
Recognize shape, dtype, and copy/view pitfalls when preparing model inputs.

mentalModel.text: A NumPy array is a typed block of values with a shape. Vectorized operations describe work on whole arrays, letting optimized numerical code process many values without writing a Python loop for each element.

concepts.title: Shape tells you what each axis means

blocks.title: Inspect a small array
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(X.shape)
print(X.ndim)
print(X.dtype)
print(X.sum(axis=0))

blocks.text: Expected output is `(2, 3)`, `2`, an integer dtype such as `int64`, and `[5 7 9]`. The array has two rows and three columns. `axis=0` reduces the row axis, leaving one sum per column. `axis=1` would return one sum per row: `[6 15]`.

blocks.title: Reading shapes
rows: n rows, d features per row
Different shapes even if values look similar
Can change broadcasting and downstream APIs

blocks.text: Always confirm the semantic meaning of each axis. A shape alone does not say whether a dimension represents samples, time, channels, classes, or features.

blocks.title: Apply one transformation to many values
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([0.2, 0.5, 0.9])
adjusted = scores * 100 + 5
print(adjusted)

blocks.text: Expected output: `[25. 55. 95.]`. NumPy applies multiplication and addition elementwise through optimized array operations. A Python loop can be clear for branching or irregular objects, but for large numeric arrays vectorization is often faster and more compact.

blocks.problem: An inference preprocessor normalizes one million numeric feature values.
reasoning: A Python loop executes the arithmetic operation at Python level for each element.
A NumPy expression applies the same transformation to the array using optimized compiled loops.
Check output shape, dtype, missing values, and numerical equivalence before comparing speed. Vectorization may allocate additional intermediate arrays, so memory also matters.
blocks.outcome: Use vectorization for regular numerical transformations, but inspect allocations as well as runtime.

blocks.title: Scale each feature column
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])
scale = np.array([10, 100])
print(X * scale)

blocks.text: Output: `[[ 10 200] [ 30 400] [ 50 600]]`. The matrix has shape `(3, 2)` and the scale vector has shape `(2,)`. NumPy aligns dimensions from the right; the vector matches the two-column dimension and is applied to each row.

blocks.title: Broadcasting rule
rows: That dimension can be expanded logically
It is treated like a size of 1
The operation raises a shape error

blocks.title: A broadcast can be legal but semantically wrong
blocks.content: If predictions have shape `(n, 1)` and labels have shape `(n,)`, combining them can produce an `(n, n)` result instead of n pairwise results. Inspect shapes and intentionally reshape arrays before arithmetic.

blocks.text: NumPy arrays usually store values in a fixed dtype. Mixing numbers and strings may coerce an array to a string/object representation, which can use more memory and disable efficient numerical operations. Inspect `dtype` at ingestion boundaries.

blocks.title: Make the intended shape and dtype explicit
blocks.source:
values = np.asarray([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
column = values.reshape(-1, 1)
print(values.shape, column.shape, values.dtype)

blocks.text: Expected output: `(3,) (3, 1) float32`. `reshape` changes the logical shape without changing the number of elements. Some operations return a view sharing underlying memory; others allocate a copy. If mutation matters, do not assume two arrays are independent—check the operation's behavior or copy explicitly.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: Vectorized expressions reduce Python overhead but can create large temporary arrays. A loop can be clearer for irregular control flow or small inputs. Use the simplest implementation that fits memory and has measured performance.

revisionSheet.text: Shape is the length of each axis; ndim is the number of axes; dtype describes element representation.
`axis=0` usually reduces rows and leaves columns; `axis=1` reduces columns and leaves rows for a 2-D matrix.
Broadcasting aligns dimensions from the right; dimensions must match or be 1.
Vectorization is not a guarantee of low memory: intermediate arrays and dtype changes matter.

questions.prompt: An array has shape `(100, 8)`. What does that normally describe for a tabular feature matrix?
questions.explanation: A two-dimensional array shape lists its first dimension then its second, often samples and features for a feature matrix.

questions.prompt: For `X` with shape `(3, 2)`, what shape does `X.sum(axis=0)` produce?
questions.explanation: Reducing axis 0 combines the three rows and leaves one result per column.

questions.prompt: Why can broadcasting `predictions` shaped `(n, 1)` with labels shaped `(n,)` be dangerous?

options.text: It can create an `(n, n)` array by pairing each prediction with every label
NumPy automatically detects intended row pairing

questions.explanation: Right-aligned shape rules can broadcast `(n,1)` and `(n,)` to `(n,n)`; reshape the labels or predictions deliberately.

questions.prompt: What is a common benefit of vectorized NumPy operations?

options.text: They often avoid Python-level loops for regular numeric work
They remove the need to inspect dtype

questions.explanation: Vectorization uses optimized array operations, but performance and allocations depend on the operation.

questions.prompt: Two arrays with the same shape necessarily use the same dtype.
questions.explanation: Shape describes dimensions; dtype separately describes how values are represented.

questions.prompt: A legal broadcasting operation is always semantically correct for the application.
questions.explanation: Shape compatibility only defines whether NumPy can perform the operation; it cannot know what each axis means.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A model metric unexpectedly returns a matrix instead of one error per row. What NumPy issue would you inspect?
strongAnswerPoints: Print the shapes of predictions, labels, and intermediate expressions.
Check for `(n,1)` versus `(n,)` alignment and reshape intentionally.
Confirm the final output shape and compare a tiny hand-calculated example.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would log each shape. If predictions are `(n,1)` and labels `(n,)`, right-aligned broadcasting may produce `(n,n)`. I would reshape one operand and test a small example against expected pairwise errors.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A preprocessing step runs quickly on a small batch but crashes on a large batch with memory exhaustion.
strongAnswerPoints: Look for repeated copies and large intermediate arrays.
Check dtype and array shape, and consider chunked operations when a full array does not fit comfortably.
Measure peak memory as well as runtime after the change.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Vectorized operations can create full-size intermediates. I would inspect allocation and dtype, avoid unnecessary copies, or process bounded chunks while preserving numerical behavior.
